title: OpenClaw launches an AI performance benchmark that it argues is more realistic than others
summary: OpenClaw, working with a host of other industry players including Hugging Face, Nvidia, Red Hat, Google and Amazon, Tuesday rolled out an AI performance benchmark called ShellBench. OpenClaw’s position is that the benchmark will compare various AI models (it will soon look at a total of 24) and test them on complex queries, ones that should better replicate the kind of complicated tasks that an enterprise would perform. “Ask an AI agent to summarize a document, and it will probably do a decent job. Ask it to reconcile a handful of receipts against a spreadsheet, check which information is current, flag a suspicious payment request, and explain how it reached its answer? Maybe not so well,” said the OpenClaw post describing the new benchmark . “This kind of realistic test, one that expects an agent not just to find the right information but also to keep track of it along the way, is exactly what we’re launching ShellBench to evaluate.” Analysts and consultants said the new benchmark findings appear initially to be more useful than existing AI performance benchmarks, but it is less clear how useful those results will be. Thomas Randall , a research director at Infotech, said that he sees ShellBench as focusing on those who are building and configuring agents directly, but most enterprises instead buy their AI capabilities from various large AI vendors. “They are choosing capabilities within an enterprise platform, often with limited control over the underlying model or agent configuration. For these organizations, ShellBench offers little direct use,” Randall said. “ShellBench giving a strong score for an underlying model does not tell us the quality of output from a solution built on it. The tasks ShellBench tests are skewed toward personal knowledge work rather than heavy enterprise workflows that buyers typically evaluate for.” Are results reproducible? title: Where the software development bottleneck went
summary: It’s not often you get to talk about potato chips twice in one year in a tech column, but here we are. Back in January, I discussed a fascinating podcast that featured a guy from Frito-Lay , who had the marvelous job of speeding up the potato chip production line. In the podcast, the Frito-Lay guy, Brendan O’Donohoe, discusses Goldratt’s Theory of Constraints — the notion that all processes are limited by a small number of constraints. In my column, I noted that coding is no longer the major constraint in software development, thanks to AI, and I said that figuring out what software projects to do next would become the new hard part. Well, I was wrong about that. I was right about one thing — coding isn’t the bottleneck anymore. I had a laugh with some friends the other day. For years they used the planning poker method of estimating projects, and it worked pretty well for them. I use the past tense because they don’t use it anymore. Over the past few months, every project they tried to specify turned out to be a “1”. Coding agents can write even major product features in time spans best measured in hours, not weeks or months. Trying to figure out how long something would take had become moot, so planning poker became pointless. Stuck in code review What I was wrong about was that developers would no longer be the bottleneck. It turns out that we still are — only in a different place. Faros , a software engineering analytics platform, has shown that the bottleneck still lies in the development team’s lap , but not in the coding phase. Code is being written at such a breakneck pace that the work is stacking up in the code review stage. It used to be that teams could review code much faster than it could be written, so they monitored metrics like “Mean Time in Review (MTiR).” Teams would work to keep that time down, meaning code was reviewed quickly and efficiently. title: Seven key features of AI governance platforms
summary: Ask leaders what they prioritize in AI governance, and many will start by discussing employee policies and guidelines. Communicating AI guardrails, business objectives, and best practices to employees is important for balancing AI strategy with controls . But as pressure mounts to deliver AI business value and drive employee adoption , organizations must address additional risk areas. Leaders in IT, security, and risk management also are worried about shadow AI , data access privileges, intellectual property leaks, AI debt , and increasing costs . “The CIO should hold the keys for data access, privilege management, and security,” says Gerrit Kazmaier, president of product and technology at Workday . “The biggest challenge for any CIO is how they can secure AI, trust that any AI is behaving lawfully based on the governance workflows, and determine which agents are auditable, traceable, and secure.” What is AI governance? You don’t have to brainstorm what goes into AI governance. TDWI defines AI governance broadly as “a set of policies, processes, roles, and controls an organization puts in place to ensure its AI systems behave as intended, produce outcomes that are fair and reliable, and operate within legal and ethical boundaries.” Some AI governance best practices include inventorying use cases, assigning ownership responsibilities to AI agent owners, and integrating data governance practices . There are also standards to review. The NIST AI 100-1 standard , known as the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, has a Govern category with seven subcategories covering legal and regulatory requirements, trustworthy AI, risk-based procedures, monitoring, inventory of AI systems, and life-cycle management. Other related standards include the ISO/IEC AI Standards and Cloud Security Alliance’s AI Control Matrix . title: Cisco and OpenAI dispatch AI agents to shield vulnerable systems before permanent patches arrive
summary: Autonomous AI agents are rapidly and dramatically transforming the cybersecurity landscape for both defenders and adversaries. In hopes of giving security teams a head start and pitting machine against machine, Cisco and OpenAI have released a new open source project, dubbed Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”). The Shirudo platform launches small, temporary mitigations to help protect systems until patches can be deployed. AI agents can replace flawed code with fixed code, which human teams can test and approve (or not), then deploy, setting boundaries and holding onto the keys, with no need for a hard reset. The project has already been proven to block a Java4Shell exploit attempt against the search and analytics platform Elasticsearch, while the site continued to run as usual. Need to buy time “For years, we’ve treated security like a coat of paint,” Cisco president and CPO Jeetu Patel wrote in a blog post . “You first build infrastructure, then wrap security around it.” But, he asserted, this approach is “fundamentally mismatched” to AI. Security should live inside the infrastructure itself. “If protection sits outside the system, it’s always a step behind,” he said. He noted that AI agents are getting better at discovering security vulnerabilities; for instance, startup Calif used AI to help discover the PHP2Shell flaw and a major Java bug . Dovetailing with this, the agents themselves are both a risk vector and an adversarial actor. Attackers are using swarms of them to exploit discovered flaws; with both PHP2Shell and Java4shell, campaigns were underway “within a day of disclosure, if not before,” he pointed out. Flaws unfold over minutes and hours, as opposed to the days and weeks of the past, but permanent fixes take time to build, test, and roll out. “We need ways to shield systems and buy our teams time to get patches in place,” Patel said. title: The Alien Space of Science: Sampling Coherent but Cognitively Unavailable Research Directions
summary: Can artificial intelligence suggest research directions that scientists are unlikely to consider? The Alien Space of Science approaches this question by separating two properties of an idea: whether its components fit together and whether an existing research community is likely to combine them. From 16,068 papers on language models, the authors construct a vocabulary of concepts and search for promising combinations beyond familiar patterns. The resulting portfolios are more diverse than those produced by the tested language-model baselines, while a retrospective experiment recovers combinations that subsequently appeared in published research. These findings make the method an interesting complement to conventional scientific ideation. They also raise a precise question about what has been measured. An unfamiliar combination is not necessarily inaccessible to human thought, and a persuasive research report is not yet a verified discovery. The strongest contribution is a practical way to broaden the search for ideas, with explicit trade-offs between novelty, coherence and the evidence needed to establish scientific value.

title: Prompting AI to be ‘thorough’ can drive sandbox escapes, Anthropic says
summary: Prompt wording meant to make AI agents more resourceful, such as telling them to search thoroughly or invoking authority, sharply raises the odds they will reach outside a poorly secured sandbox, Anthropic has found in its latest evaluation. The evaluation, called Siren, gives Claude models routine dev-ops tasks inside deliberately weakened sandboxes and places a “honeypot,” such as a credential, file, or emulated internet service, outside the boundary, Anthropic researchers Oscar O’Rahilly and Darya Kaviani wrote in a blog post . Anthropic tested six Claude models, from Mythos 5 to the 5.5 series, without the safeguards that ship in its products. The tests covered more than 1,700 scenarios in 26 sandboxes built on tools including Docker, gVisor, and QEMU. Most of the weaknesses are misconfigurations modeled on public reports, the company said. Wording mattered more than deadlines Anthropic’s researchers tested different types of instructions, which they called “tempters”. Some increased urgency by introducing deadlines or the consequences of failure. Others encouraged agents to search extensively or gave them broad authority over their machines. “Some tempters give the model broad authority over its own machine. Others tell it to search thoroughly, on that machine or more widely, and list what it checked,” the researchers wrote. Removing deadlines and stated costs of failure changed the rate of reaching outside by no more than about six percentage points, the post said. Removing the wording that asked for thoroughness and asserted authority had a far larger effect, cutting reach rates by 23 to 26 points in five of the six models, the researchers wrote. title: Anthropic lets you install Claude ‘artifacts’ as Mac apps
summary: Anthropic is now rolling out beta access to a new Claude feature that lets you save some of what it does as live apps on Macs, using “artifacts.” What’s new is that you can take an artifact and install it as an app on your Mac. The same trick works on Windows systems too. The move makes Apple’s recent decision to give users more control over which apps and AI services have access to their data a lot more understandable. An artifact is different from a standard Claude chat. Essentially, it is a standalone piece of output Claude builds; it can be a web page, interactive tool, document, slide deck, or design. You can open it, use it, edit it, and share it. Available on all Anthropic plans, artifacts exist in a separate section of the Claude sidebar, called, appropriately enough, Artifacts. How to build an artifact It’s pretty simple to make one of these things. First, develop a complex question that defines the result. It could be to request a slide deck capturing the environmental consequences of data center deployments globally tracked over time graphed against consumer energy prices. You could ask for that to be generated using green and yellow nature colors, or even request a little widget that can predict future data based on different criteria. Once the AI has finished working on the document, you can go in and edit it. For example, you may choose to take a screen grab of the trees marching against the tower of Saruman in the Lord of the Rings movie trilogy as a background image for one of the slides, or perhaps greenwash the entire deck with pictures of rainbows and flowers. When it’s done, you can save or share the artifact. I did that, and you can download the resulting slide deck as a PDF here , but only for a limited time. When you share an artifact and install it as an app on your Mac, it gets its own icon and opens inside its own window. title: One of the best AI-proof businesses is a data-rich business.
summary: In this solo episode, I lay out how I think about building an AI-proof business now that anyone can press a few buttons and spin up a company in seconds. Layoffs keep coming, people copy products pixel for pixel, and I still see more opportunity than ever. I walk through eight categories: atoms, permission, attention, timing, belonging, liquidity, unique data, and outcomes. I share examples like Hampton, final.com, and Cars & Bids, say how I'd rank the categories, and show how to mix them. If you're an employee looking at a startup or a founder worried about getting copied, this episode gives you a map for building something with value when AI makes software, content, and answers almost free. Key Points • Physical businesses hold up against overnight clones, and I expect their valuations to rise as tech money moves in. • Licenses, regulation, and preferred-vendor deals are permission that a copycat has a hard time getting on day one. • Media is underrated, and AI lets you run a content machine around a micro niche. • A first mover's product may be easy to copy, while the data, brand, and trust it collects stay AI-proof. • Marketplaces rank among the stickiest businesses of all time, and agents let a team of one to five run one. Section Summaries 1. Atoms and Permission Pixels are software businesses and atoms are physical ones, like a coffee shop or the plumber who fixes your clogged toilet. They're harder to run, they hold up against overnight clones, and I think their valuations go up once AI and tech money spots the moat. Permission covers licenses, regulation, and deals, so you could partner with a lawyer and handle marketing, growth, and AI while they run the firm. 3.
